fontaenenteich.name: Fountain Pond
fontaenenteich.shortDescription: The Fountain Pond is the deliberately created, natural-looking basin of the Great Fountain and forms the calm final landscape space of the historic water displays.
fontaenenteich.longDescription: The Fountain Pond looks like a natural park lake, but it is the product of deliberate landscape and hydraulic design. Here the long sequence of water descending from the Hercules reaches its final spatial setting. The Peneus Cascades feed the area, paths and vegetation frame the water, and the nozzle of the Great Fountain sits within the pond. The contrast is carefully staged: after cascades, waterfalls and artificial ravines, the water appears to settle into a horizontal surface before rising in the finale as a jet more than fifty metres high. The pond is therefore both a landscape picture and part of the machinery of the display.
fontaenenteich.history: Kassel visitor material places the creation of the natural-looking artificial pond in the middle of the eighteenth century. Later landscape-garden transformations integrated it more fully into the picturesque lower park. The powerful Great Fountain developed in the eighteenth century and the Romantic water route added later made the pond the final gathering space for water from several historical phases. Its history therefore overlaps both Baroque hydraulic ambition and the later landscape style.
fontaenenteich.architecture: The banks are softly shaped rather than monumentally walled. Beneath and around the visible water surface, however, supply routes, drainage, the fountain nozzle and pressure infrastructure belong to the technical system. The pond is therefore simultaneously water body, visual stage and hydraulic working space. It must be kept distinct from the Lac farther east. The promoted OSM graph and World Heritage inventory treat the two as separate waters with different functions.
fontaenenteich.culturalSignificance: As the final space of the water displays, the Fountain Pond unites engineering with an apparently natural landscape. It is one of the clearest places to show that "nature" at Wilhelmshöhe is often designed and technically supported. The sudden vertical fountain gains much of its impact from the quiet horizontal surface that precedes it.
fontaenenteich.restorationHistory: Banks, water-management structures and fountain infrastructure have been maintained over centuries. A detailed restoration history of the pond form and subsurface engineering will be added from specialist conservation records rather than inferred from the current appearance.
fontaenenteich.visitorContext: The pond is freely accessible throughout the year. On regular water-display days the Great Fountain begins at about 15:45. Wind can carry spray well beyond the fountain head. Paths around the water vary in gradient and surface, so the whole shoreline should not be labelled uniformly accessible. The pond is not a recreational bathing lake.
fontaenenteich.interpretation: The Fountain Pond is an excellent example of the difference between visible landscape and hidden function. A visitor sees calm water, trees and paths; beneath that scene a long hydraulic chain reaches its end. A digital guide should therefore offer both a landscape view and an engineering view linking reservoir, inflows and fountain nozzle. Comparison with the Lac is essential. Both can appear natural, yet the Fountain Pond is tightly coupled to the historic fountain mechanism whereas the Lac organises a separate landscape space around the palace, Mulang and Löwenburg. Ecologically, the pond is now also habitat, so management must balance heritage form, water quality, vegetation and technical requirements. The knowledge base does not make unsupported ecological claims, but it records that a historic park water body can carry several functions at once. The City of Kassel now states the distinction explicitly: water leaves the Fountain Pond and continues to the palace pond called the Lac. The Fountain Pond therefore remains a separate hydraulic and mapped node.

ballhaus.name: Ballhaus
ballhaus.shortDescription: The understated Ballhaus beside Wilhelmshöhe Palace was built in 1808–1810 as Jérôme Bonaparte’s court theatre and received its richly decorated Electoral ballroom interior in 1828–1830.
ballhaus.longDescription: The Ballhaus is a building whose exterior and interior effects differ strikingly. From the park it appears comparatively restrained, a plastered structure close to the palace. Inside, however, the main hall opens as a richly decorated ceremonial space with half-columns, a shallow barrel vault, painted ornament and a gallery. This contrast reflects the building's changing functions. It began as a theatre and later became a representative ballroom. Today the historic interior is normally encountered during concerts, readings and other special events rather than as a continuously open museum. The building therefore adds performing arts and courtly sociability to a park often described mainly through landscape, water and collections.
ballhaus.history: The young Leo von Klenze designed the court theatre for Jérôme Bonaparte in 1808, during the period when Kassel was the capital of the Kingdom of Westphalia; performances began by 1810. After the restoration of Electoral Hesse, Johann Conrad Bromeis substantially transformed the building in 1828–1830 for Elector Wilhelm II, converting it into a ballroom. The present interior character belongs largely to this second phase. The building thus spans two sharply different political regimes and demonstrates how court architecture could be adapted rather than discarded after political change.
ballhaus.architecture: The official monument inventory describes a simple plastered exterior with attic and hipped roof. The hall, approximately twenty-five by seventeen metres, is articulated by half-columns and a shallow barrel-vaulted ceiling. At the south end is a gallery or buffet-room arrangement. Decorative painting after Bromeis includes coffering, fruit garlands, a parrot frieze and Arcadian motifs. The relative sobriety of the exterior makes the ceremonial interior all the more surprising.
ballhaus.culturalSignificance: The Ballhaus expands the cultural history of Wilhelmshöhe beyond the visual arts. Theatre, music, dance and formal gathering were integral parts of seasonal court life. Its layered design also prevents the building from being assigned to one architect or one political moment: Klenze's theatre and Bromeis's ballroom are both essential to its identity.
ballhaus.restorationHistory: A major restoration is documented for 1975–1984. The historic interior and decorative scheme have been conserved as significant fabric. More detailed conservation information can be added from restoration records in a later phase without weakening the secure chronology already established by the official monument inventory.
ballhaus.visitorContext: According to current Hessen Kassel Heritage information, the Ballhaus is open only for special events. It is wheelchair accessible and assistance dogs are permitted. A normal park visit should therefore not promise spontaneous interior access. The surrounding exterior remains part of the freely accessible palace area.
ballhaus.interpretation: Its position beside the palace explains an important part of its role. A stay at Wilhelmshöhe involved more than walking through gardens: theatre, music, dancing and social encounter required specialised interior spaces. Together with the palace and Great Greenhouse, the Ballhaus forms an ensemble in which residence, entertainment and landscape experience interacted. The conversion from theatre to ballroom is especially instructive because it shows institutional resilience across the fall of the Kingdom of Westphalia and restoration of the Electorate. In a digital guide the modest façade can be paired with interior images or plans so that visitors understand why the building is more significant than its exterior suggests. Current opening information should remain separate from historical description: a monument can be deeply documented even when its interior is closed on an ordinary day.

gewaechshaus.name: Great Greenhouse
gewaechshaus.shortDescription: The Great Greenhouse, begun in 1822, is among the early European glass-and-iron greenhouse structures and still serves the seasonal overwintering of exotic plants from the Bergpark.
gewaechshaus.longDescription: The Great Greenhouse is simultaneously a plant house, a technical building and a place of courtly display. Elector Wilhelm II commissioned it from 1822 for a valuable collection of frost-sensitive plants. Large glazed surfaces brought light into the long wings while a sophisticated heating system made winter cultivation possible in northern Hesse. The building was not merely storage for plants. The central salon could be used by the Elector to receive guests, combining tea, architecture and exotic botany in a carefully staged experience. Its continuing plant function gives the building an unusual continuity between historic design and present-day park management.
gewaechshaus.history: Johann Conrad Bromeis designed the greenhouse in 1822. Hessen Kassel Heritage emphasises its place among the earliest glass-and-metal structures of its kind in Europe. The original central section was round; around 1888 it was altered into the present rectangular form, and warm-house plants were accommodated there. This alteration is an important historical layer rather than a defect in an otherwise fixed "original" design. The building records changing greenhouse technologies and changing requirements of the living collection.
gewaechshaus.architecture: The long transparent wings and central block are organised around maximum daylight, controllable temperature and practical movement of plants. Glass, metal structure, heating and ventilation form one technical system. At the same time the building is composed as an architectural object within the palace landscape. Its apparently delicate envelope depends on substantial infrastructure and maintenance. The later rectangular central block should be read as part of the building's nineteenth-century development.
gewaechshaus.culturalSignificance: The greenhouse links the dendrological and botanical collections of the Bergpark directly with architectural and technological history. Exotic plants could become enduring elements of a princely garden only if overwintering, transport, heating and specialist care were organised. The building therefore represents the often invisible labour and infrastructure behind a living collection.
gewaechshaus.restorationHistory: The central block was altered around 1888, and the greenhouse has necessarily received technical adaptation and conservation throughout its working life. A later tree-and-collection phase should document the heating history and the relationship between individual plant groups and the building in more detail.
gewaechshaus.visitorContext: Current operator information states that the Great Greenhouse is open from 1 November to 31 March, Tuesday to Sunday from 10:00 to 17:00, with last admission at 16:30; it is closed during the summer months. It is wheelchair accessible. Admission is included in the Wilhelmshöhe day ticket. These are volatile visitor facts and are stored with verification date 2026-08-27.
gewaechshaus.interpretation: The seasonal opening rhythm is meaningful rather than arbitrary. In winter, when sensitive plants are protected inside, the collection is visible in the building; during the warmer season part of the plant material returns to outdoor settings and the greenhouse is closed. That seasonal movement connects the architecture directly to the later tree and plant catalogue. The Great Greenhouse should also be clearly distinguished from the Orangerie in the Karlsaue, which is a different park complex in Kassel and should not be promoted as a Bergpark node. A strong interpretation combines botanical history with engineering: a purely decorative description of "exotic plants" would hide the heating, glazing, transport and horticultural labour that made the collection possible, while a purely technical description would miss the greenhouse's role in courtly display. Hessen Kassel Heritage explicitly places the Orangery Palace in Karlsaue Park. Omitting an Orangery node from the Bergpark inventory is therefore a deliberate spatial distinction, not a content gap.

lac.name: Lac
lac.shortDescription: The Lac is a distinct landscape lake east and south-east of the palace area and must not be confused with the Fountain Pond used by the Great Fountain.
lac.longDescription: The Lac belongs to the landscape-garden transformation of the lower park. Its broad water surface, curving banks and surrounding tree groups create a very different effect from the technically focused Fountain Pond. The lake participates in the visual spaces around the palace, Löwenburg and Mulang, binding architecture into a softer, English-influenced landscape. Historic mapping and the current promoted OpenStreetMap geometry confirm that the Lac and Fountain Pond are separate bodies of water. Keeping them separate is therefore essential both for navigation and for understanding the development of the garden.
lac.history: The landscape creation of the Lac is associated with the transformation under Landgrave Wilhelm IX and the work of Heinrich Christoph Jussow in the late eighteenth century. The lake reshaped or absorbed earlier valley and water conditions and became a major organising element of the mature landscape park. Areas connected with Mulang and the former pheasantry lay nearby, so the Lac must be understood in relation to a wider south-eastern park zone rather than as an isolated ornamental pond.
lac.architecture: The lake has no monumental architectural frame. Its architecture is the designed shoreline itself: banks, paths, planted groups, open water and sight lines combine to make a sequence of landscape pictures. The relative invisibility of engineering is part of the effect. This distinguishes it from Baroque basins and from the Fountain Pond, where the hydraulic function of the Great Fountain is central even when it is visually concealed.
lac.culturalSignificance: The Lac makes the shift from axial Baroque display to large-scale landscape garden especially legible. It links the palace, Mulang, Löwenburg and lower park spaces through views and walking routes. Its significance lies less in one object at its centre than in the moving sequence around its edges.
lac.restorationHistory: Banks, water management and vegetation are maintained as components of the historic garden. A detailed construction and restoration chronology will be added from the park-maintenance and conservation documentation rather than inferred from current shoreline form.
lac.visitorContext: Paths around the Lac are freely accessible. Individual sections can be uneven or soft in wet weather. The lake is not a bathing facility. Because it covers an area rather than a single point, accessibility and walking distances must eventually be calculated from actual shoreline-path geometry rather than from the representative node coordinate.
lac.interpretation: The Lac is a strong test case for precise spatial modelling. A centre point is useful for orientation but insufficient for route and accessibility calculations. In the later paths phase, shoreline routes should become explicit edges with surface and gradient data. The lake is also best experienced through movement: views of tree groups, lawns and nearby architecture change as the visitor walks, unlike the frontal relationship of the main palace-to-Hercules axis. Semantically it should be connected to Mulang as well as to Löwenburg and the palace. That makes the historical south-eastern park legible as a network of water, working-estate buildings and picturesque architecture. Above all, the dataset must preserve the distinction from Fountain Pond: the Lac is primarily a landscape lake; Fountain Pond is a terminal space and technical component of the historic water displays. The current City of Kassel interpretation resolves an important naming issue explicitly: the romantic palace pond, the Schlossteich, is the water body called the Lac. Water reaches it only after leaving the Fountain Pond through deliberately constructed but natural-looking cascades. ‘Schlossteich’ is therefore a documented alias of the Lac, not of the Fountain Pond. The city dates the transformation of a small fishpond into the Lac to 1785–1791 under Heinrich Christoph Jussow and records the outlet at its eastern end in 1789. This primary source confirms both the spatial distinction between the two ponds and their sequence within the water system.

mulang.name: Mulang Village / Mou-lang
mulang.shortDescription: The chinoiserie park village Mou-lang, begun around 1781/82, combined exoticising garden scenery with a working dairy estate; the official monument record indicates that thirteen historic buildings survive.
mulang.longDescription: Mulang is not a single pavilion but a historical ensemble at the south-eastern edge of the park. Landgrave Friedrich II had a "Chinese village" created here in the 1780s. In eighteenth-century Europe, chinoiserie was not an accurate representation of Chinese architecture. It was a European imaginative construction informed by travel accounts, porcelain imagery and publications such as those of William Chambers. At Mou-lang that exoticising visual language was combined with practical estate functions. Alongside the Pagoda and other picturesque buildings stood houses and agricultural structures belonging to a dairy operation intended to provide milk, butter and cheese for the court. The village therefore joined theatrical scenery with real work.
mulang.history: The ensemble developed under Friedrich II from about 1781/82. Court gardener Daniel August Schwarzkopf is associated with its planning, while Simon Louis du Ry and later court architects influenced individual buildings. Under Wilhelm IX parts of the ensemble were altered from around 1791, often in a more restrained classical direction. The official monument inventory records thirteen surviving historic buildings from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The Pagoda remains the most conspicuous marker, while former service buildings have been converted, adapted or lost. In the nineteenth century the name Mulang also spread to the neighbouring villa district.
mulang.architecture: Architecturally Mulang is deliberately heterogeneous. Small dwellings, dairy and kitchen buildings, former cow and sheep sheds and the Pagoda use timber framing, plastered walls, tent-like roofs and, in some cases, chinoiserie decoration. The buildings originally stood more freely in meadow-like surroundings. Roads, hedges and later residential development now divide the ensemble more strongly. This changed setting is itself part of the site's history and should not be digitally erased in pursuit of an imaginary pristine scene.
mulang.culturalSignificance: Mulang documents European chinoiserie, court agriculture and the social infrastructure required to maintain a large landscape park. Modern interpretation should not romanticise its historical terminology as if it represented China itself. The "China" of Mou-lang was a European projection. At the same time the surviving working buildings are authentic evidence of labour, animals, food production and service behind the princely landscape. Current HKK interpretation explicitly contextualises the chinoiserie critically as a European projection; that perspective is part of the ensemble’s source record.
mulang.restorationHistory: Several buildings were altered, repurposed or replaced during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; some have disappeared. The Pagoda was renovated repeatedly, and former agricultural and residential buildings were modernised for new uses. Despite those changes, the ensemble remains protected and forms part of the World Heritage landscape.
mulang.visitorContext: The park village lies along and near Mulangstraße. Many of the buildings are homes or otherwise not open as public interiors. Visitors should respect private use and view the ensemble from public paths and roads. The Pagoda is an especially useful orientation point. A digital guide must not encourage entry onto private plots simply because a building has historical significance.
mulang.interpretation: Mulang is best represented as an ensemble node with additional subnodes for major surviving or ruinous structures such as the Pagoda and Bagatelle. That structure prevents the decorative pavilion from eclipsing the economic life of the village. A dairy estate required workers, livestock, storage, kitchen space and maintenance; chinoiserie and daily labour existed side by side. The present-day residential layer adds another ethical consideration: this is not an abandoned museum village. Good visitor information distinguishes publicly visible heritage from private occupation. In interpretation, three levels should remain visible at once—the European fantasy of chinoiserie, the real productive function of the estate, and the later transformation of the area into a residential park edge. Their coexistence is precisely what gives Mulang its historical depth.

entenfang.name: Entenfang / Duck Pond
entenfang.shortDescription: The Entenfang is a historic small park pond in the south-western area; the task label "Entenpfuhl" could not be confirmed as a separate named mapped feature and is retained only as an uncertain alias.
entenfang.longDescription: The Entenfang is one of the quieter water bodies that structure the Bergpark beyond the famous display route. Unlike the Great Fountain or cascades, it is not defined by a dramatic hydraulic performance. Its value lies in its relationship to woodland, paths and the broader network of historic ponds and channels. During the Phase-1 spatial survey, OpenStreetMap contained a mapped historic pond named Entenfang but no separate point or water body named Entenpfuhl. The knowledge layer therefore follows the physical evidence and uses Entenfang as the node while preserving Entenpfuhl only for search and future archival checking.
entenfang.history: The detailed creation and use history of the pond is less well documented in the official sources evaluated so far than the major waterworks. The name may suggest a historical relationship to ducks or duck catching, but no specific practice is asserted here without primary documentation. This is an intentional limit rather than a gap filled by plausible-sounding invention.
entenfang.architecture: The pond is shaped as a landscape water body rather than a monumental architectural basin. Its modest scale and surrounding vegetation give it an ecological and atmospheric role different from the formal waterworks. The mapped geometry, rather than a speculative architectural reconstruction, is the appropriate starting point for later spatial work.
entenfang.culturalSignificance: Entenfang demonstrates that water at Wilhelmshöhe is not used only as dynastic spectacle. Small ponds, channels and wet areas also organise the landscape and contribute to the variety of park environments.
entenfang.restorationHistory: Maintenance belongs to broader garden and water management. A specific historical restoration chronology has not yet been established and is not invented.
entenfang.visitorContext: The pond can be approached on park paths. Banks are not presented as bathing or recreation areas, and nearby surfaces may be soft after wet weather. Visitors should remain on paths where required and respect habitat and heritage management.
entenfang.interpretation: The naming uncertainty is deliberately visible in the dataset. A later archival source may show whether Entenpfuhl was an historical alternative name, a neighbouring locality or simply a modern mislabelling. Until then, merging the terms as proven synonyms would reduce rather than improve accuracy. This is a model for handling uncertain names elsewhere in the park: preserve the search term, attach a confidence note and keep the spatially verified entity distinct.

neuer-wasserfall.name: New Waterfall
neuer-wasserfall.shortDescription: The New Waterfall, created in 1823–1828, was the last major historical waterwork added to the Bergpark; unlike the other historic water features, it has not been operational for decades.
neuer-wasserfall.longDescription: The New Waterfall lies in the northern part of the park and belongs to the final major phase of the historic waterworks. Basalt tuff and shaped terrain again create the image of a dramatic natural fall. The crucial difference is its present condition. It is not part of the regular functioning water-display sequence. UNESCO explicitly identifies the New Waterfall as the exception to the otherwise surviving operability of the historic water features. That non-operational status should be stated plainly in visitor information rather than hidden behind an idealised historical description.
neuer-wasserfall.history: The official Hessian monument inventory dates construction to 1823–1828 and associates the work with Karl Steinhöfer and Johann Conrad Bromeis, during the period of Elector Wilhelm II. Popular accounts sometimes highlight 1826 as a single date, but the knowledge base uses the broader official construction range. The feature closes the long development of major water architecture from the Baroque Hercules system through the picturesque eighteenth-century waterfalls into the nineteenth century.
neuer-wasserfall.architecture: The waterfall is an artificial rock landscape built with basalt tuff and supplied by a network of channels and ditches. Its technical components were designed to make controlled water appear as natural force. The surviving dry structure still records this relationship between engineered ground and picturesque effect even though the hydraulic display is not operating.
neuer-wasserfall.culturalSignificance: The New Waterfall is important precisely because it complicates a simple story of perfect continuity. The World Heritage water system is extraordinarily functional, but not every historic element survives in operating condition. The feature demonstrates the chronological depth of the network and the conservation choices involved in maintaining a complex landscape monument.
neuer-wasserfall.restorationHistory: The water function has been out of operation for decades. The built and landscape fabric remains protected. This dataset does not assume that reactivation is either technically straightforward or a conservation objective. Any future restoration would require specialist hydraulic and heritage assessment.
neuer-wasserfall.visitorContext: The site can be visited as a dry historical feature, but visitors should not expect a scheduled waterfall. It lies away from the principal water-display route, and access may involve slopes and less prominent paths. Interpretation should distinguish clearly between historical function and present operation.
neuer-wasserfall.interpretation: The non-operational status also teaches an important conservation principle. "Not operating" is not the same as "destroyed" or "unimportant." Channels, rockwork and traces of the former system can remain significant even when the original effect is not reproduced. A digital reconstruction may show the historical flow, but it must be labelled as reconstruction rather than implying live functionality. The source record is unusually robust because an older monument inventory already describes long-term non-operation and UNESCO currently names the New Waterfall as the exception in an otherwise functioning system. The term "Neue Wasserkunst" should not be turned into a fabricated map point. It can describe the historical conceptual group of later waterworks, while the spatial node here represents the physically mapped New Waterfall. World Heritage Committee decision 37 COM 8B.33 gives unusually clear evidence for the present functional status: at inscription, every water feature in the ensemble except the New Waterfall remained operable. The node is therefore recorded as surviving but non-functional. ‘Neue Wasserkunst’ remains a historical/conceptual search alias; without separately verified geometry it is not promoted as a second point. This avoids both calling an extant dry structure ‘lost’ and turning a historical umbrella term into a fabricated landmark.

halle-des-sokrates.name: Hall of Socrates
halle-des-sokrates.shortDescription: The semicircular Hall of Socrates, built in 1813–1816 to a design by Heinrich Christoph Jussow, is a Classical resting and viewing structure near the palace and Bowling Green.
halle-des-sokrates.longDescription: The Hall of Socrates, also known in descriptions as a semicircular temple, stands in one of the more open and maintained parts of the lower park west of the palace. Its curved colonnade forms a sheltered architectural edge while remaining open to the landscape. It should not be confused with the Hermitage of Socrates in the woodland. The two features use the same philosopher's name in very different spatial and social settings. The hall is regular, public-facing and Classical; the hermitage plays with modesty, retreat and solitude.
halle-des-sokrates.history: Heinrich Christoph Jussow designed the hall, which was built between 1813 and 1816. It belongs to the later phase of landscape transformation under Elector Wilhelm I and dates shortly before the Jussow Temple. Its proximity to the palace and Bowling Green ties it more closely to courtly promenade and sociable use than to the dramatic ruin and gorge scenery of the water route.
halle-des-sokrates.architecture: The defining architectural idea is the semicircular arrangement of columns. It frames an open space without fully enclosing it. The regular Classical language is calm and ordered, creating shade, a fixed scale and a visual frame within the planted landscape. The architecture gains much of its meaning from the space in front of it rather than from an elaborate interior.
halle-des-sokrates.culturalSignificance: The hall demonstrates the variety of Classical forms in the Bergpark and the persistence of antique philosophical naming. It also shows how architecture could combine rest, view and cultural association without becoming a museum building or monument of monumental scale.
halle-des-sokrates.restorationHistory: The structure survives as a protected monument. Individual conservation interventions have not yet been reconstructed from building records and are left for a later specialist phase.
halle-des-sokrates.visitorContext: The open park structure can be experienced from the freely accessible lower grounds. The palace area is generally easier to reach than the steep upper park, but paths should not be labelled universally barrier-free without route-specific assessment.
halle-des-sokrates.interpretation: The Socrates name should be interpreted cautiously. It is evidence of the broad eighteenth- and early-nineteenth-century use of philosophers as cultural references in gardens, but the dataset does not invent a specific philosophical lesson that the architecture is supposed to embody. More productive is the comparison with the Hermitage of Socrates: one uses a regular colonnade near representative palace spaces, the other an image of solitary retreat in the woods. A semantic "Socrates reception" relationship can make that contrast discoverable. For navigation the hall is also a useful rest node in the dense lower-park cluster of palace, Ballhaus, greenhouse and Fountain Pond, even though it is not on the direct sequence of the historic water displays. The Hall appears independently in both the UNESCO nomination inventory and Kassel’s official park map. This provides a firm basis for distinguishing it from the older Hermitage of Socrates. The two places share the philosopher’s name but belong to different architectural types and social settings: here an open, socially legible colonnade on the Bowling Green, there a deliberately secluded retreat. A search for ‘Socrates’ should therefore return both places without merging their geometry or chronology.

merkurtempel.name: Temple of Mercury
merkurtempel.shortDescription: The Temple of Mercury was first built in timber in 1782/83 to a design by Simon Louis du Ry, rebuilt in stone by Johann Conrad Bromeis in 1823, and completed again with dome and figure in 2013/14 after wartime losses.
merkurtempel.longDescription: The Temple of Mercury is a small circular garden temple whose changing material history makes the long chronology of the Bergpark unusually visible. The open structure is formed by eight columns and historically belonged with a dome and a figure of Mercury. The Venus Temple at Stowe in England is commonly cited as an important model, reflecting the way English landscape-garden architecture circulated across Europe. At Wilhelmshöhe the borrowed temple type was given a different mythological identity and placed within its own woodland and water landscape. Its effect comes from the contrast between regular Classical geometry and the surrounding vegetation.
merkurtempel.history: Simon Louis du Ry designed the first version in 1782/83, when it was built in timber. In 1823 Johann Conrad Bromeis replaced that structure with a stone version. During the Second World War the dome and Mercury statue were lost. The official 2008 monument inventory therefore records an incomplete state that visitors no longer see. In 2013/14 the dome and figure were reconstructed, restoring the overall silhouette. This chronology is an important warning against treating any single historical inventory as a timeless description of a monument.
merkurtempel.architecture: The temple is an open circular structure about six metres in diameter with eight columns. The dome and central figure give the composition a vertical focus. The present fabric contains several chronological layers: the nineteenth-century stone replacement of an eighteenth-century timber building, surviving historic material, wartime loss and twenty-first-century reconstruction. That layered material biography is more accurate than assigning the entire visible monument to one construction date.
merkurtempel.culturalSignificance: The Temple of Mercury links English landscape-garden influence, classical mythology and Hessian building history. Its reconstruction also makes modern conservation visible as part of the site's biography. Mercury joins Hercules, Pluto, the Sibyl and other antique references across the park, but these names should not be forced into a single documented "route of the gods." The features arose at different dates and under changing patrons.
merkurtempel.restorationHistory: After the loss of dome and statue in the Second World War, both were reconstructed in 2013/14. The restored appearance should therefore be described as a historically informed modern completion rather than uninterrupted original fabric. This distinction is central to transparent heritage interpretation.
merkurtempel.visitorContext: The temple is accessible as an outdoor garden feature. Its position in the northern landscape park means that approaches can involve woodland paths and gradients. Regular interior opening is not relevant to the open colonnade form.
merkurtempel.interpretation: The sequence of timber temple, stone replacement, wartime damage and modern reconstruction makes this a model case for object biography. Visitors often ask whether a restored monument is "original." Here the most useful answer is chronological rather than binary. Different portions and forms belong to different periods, and each period is documented. A digital timeline can show the transformation more clearly than a single date label. The mythological name also supports thematic linking to other antique references, while source discipline prevents invention of an overarching narrative that is not historically demonstrated. This same approach can later be applied to the reconstructed tower of Löwenburg and other restored park structures. The Temple of Mercury is explicitly inventoried as a separate park staffage in the official records. Its importance therefore rests on documented heritage structure rather than on a transmitted name alone. Digital interpretation should explain the ancient god’s name as part of European garden iconography without inventing an undocumented cultic function. The surviving pavilion belongs to the dense layer of small architectural signs through which a walk repeatedly shifts among designed nature, classical reference and courtly education.

sibyllengrotte.name: Sibyl Grotto
sibyllengrotte.shortDescription: The Sibyl Grotto, created around 1780, belongs to the early sentimental landscape features of Wilhelmshöhe and combines artificial naturalism with the antique idea of prophetic Sibyls and hidden places.
sibyllengrotte.longDescription: The Sibyl Grotto is one of the smaller garden features that can easily disappear from a landmark-focused account of the Bergpark. Its name evokes the Sibyls of ancient tradition, prophetic women associated in European imagination with oracles, caves and sacred places. In a late-eighteenth-century landscape garden, a grotto provided an ideal architectural type for ideas of mystery, darkness, age and hidden knowledge. Unlike Pluto's Grotto, the Sibyl Grotto is not primarily a major station in the functioning water-display sequence. Its importance lies more in the intimate, associative experience created within the landscape.
sibyllengrotte.history: The official monument inventory dates the grotto to around 1780 and places it in the park phase associated with Simon Louis du Ry. It belongs to the same broad cultural generation as the Pyramid of Cestius, Tomb of Virgil, Hermitage of Socrates and Temple of Mercury. Later transformations under Wilhelm IX did not simply erase these earlier features; many were absorbed into the new landscape context and acquired new relationships to paths and vegetation.
sibyllengrotte.architecture: The grotto deliberately blurs the boundary between construction and nature. Stone, earth, planted setting and a darker interior can create the impression of an old place that has emerged from the terrain. Such structures were carefully made in order to hide their own artifice. The present condition must therefore be read as both architectural fabric and landscape setting.
sibyllengrotte.culturalSignificance: The Sibyl Grotto broadens the mythological and intellectual vocabulary of the park beyond monumental heroes and rulers. It shows how eighteenth-century garden design used literature, antiquity and emotional room types to shape a walk. Its small scale is precisely part of its function: discovery and intimacy replace long-distance visibility.
sibyllengrotte.restorationHistory: The structure survives as a protected feature. A detailed restoration chronology has not yet been established from primary conservation records. No claim is made that every visible stone or interior surface belongs unchanged to the first construction phase.
sibyllengrotte.visitorContext: The site can be approached as an outdoor garden feature. Small grotto interiors may be restricted for safety or conservation, so the dataset does not promise unrestricted entry. Paths in the surrounding terrain may be uneven.
sibyllengrotte.interpretation: The best thematic context is the group of learned and mythological features created around 1775–1783. Linking the Sibyl Grotto to the Hermitage, Pyramid, Tomb of Virgil and Temple of Mercury turns an easily overlooked object into part of an intelligible intellectual landscape. At the same time, each feature should retain its own date and source history. A shared antique vocabulary does not prove that the sites were designed as one continuous narrative. This distinction between thematic relationship and documented planning relationship is important for the knowledge graph.

pagode.name: Mulang Pagoda
pagode.shortDescription: The Pagoda, created around 1780/81, is the most conspicuous surviving pavilion of Mou-lang and a key example of European chinoiserie in the Bergpark.
pagode.longDescription: The Pagoda stands as the most recognisable visual marker of the historic village of Mulang. Its name and form evoke Asian architecture, but the design belongs to European chinoiserie rather than to an accurate reproduction of a Chinese building tradition. Hessen Kassel Heritage preserves an architectural survey and repainting proposal from 1825/26, and research links the broader design vocabulary to English pattern books and garden publications. The pavilion uses columns, an encircling walkway, curved roof forms and a lantern-like upper element to create an exoticising silhouette. Coloured glass and decorative details historically reinforced that effect. Modern interpretation should make the European origin of this imagined "China" explicit.
pagode.history: The Pagoda probably belonged to the earliest buildings of Mou-lang as the village developed around 1780/81 under Landgrave Friedrich II. The village combined picturesque scenery with a working dairy estate. Under Wilhelm IX parts of the ensemble were later altered, while the Pagoda remained an especially visible marker. The 1825/26 architectural documentation shows that repainting and maintenance were already part of its nineteenth-century history. Later renovations further changed colours and details.
pagode.architecture: The pavilion combines a columned perimeter, an encircling gallery or ambulatory, curved roof forms and an upper lantern. Historic colour schemes and decorative details changed over time. The surviving architectural drawings are particularly valuable because they record a dated design state rather than relying only on later photographs or modern appearance.
pagode.culturalSignificance: The Pagoda is the clearest single symbol of the chinoiserie layer of Wilhelmshöhe. Yet it must not be detached from the working buildings of Mulang. The historical ensemble placed exoticising courtly imagery beside dairy, kitchen, stable and residential functions. That juxtaposition is central to its meaning.
pagode.restorationHistory: The Pagoda has undergone repeated renovation and alteration. Not every visible feature should be assumed to belong to the first construction phase. The dataset therefore separates its approximate initial date from later documented designs and modern conservation states.
pagode.visitorContext: The exterior is clearly visible from public routes near Mulangstraße. The present village includes private homes, and visitors should not treat surrounding plots as an open-air museum. Regular interior access to the Pagoda is not guaranteed.
pagode.interpretation: The Pagoda is a strong place for critical interpretation of chinoiserie. Visitors can learn both about eighteenth-century fascination with distant cultures and about how selective, inaccurate and projective that knowledge often was. The building should also remain technically linked to the Mulang ensemble rather than becoming an isolated decorative marker. A digital comparison between the 1825/26 drawings and current appearance can make changes in colour and detail visible. This turns the pavilion into a useful case study in source-based architectural history and avoids the false idea of a single timeless "original" state. The Pagoda remains the most visible marker of the historical Mulang ensemble, but it should not be interpreted as an isolated ‘Chinese’ object. Current official HKK interpretation of Mulang stresses that the park village emerged from a European exoticising construction. The knowledge base therefore reads the Pagoda simultaneously as surviving staffage, as part of a real working and residential ensemble, and as evidence of a problematic history of projection. This context prevents eighteenth-century chinoiserie from being mistaken for an authentic representation of Chinese architecture.

kleiner-herkules.name: Little Hercules
kleiner-herkules.shortDescription: The Little Hercules consists of masonry remains from an early project begun in 1696 and documents the planning history that preceded the later monumental Hercules and Octagon.
kleiner-herkules.longDescription: South of the present Hercules complex are modest masonry remains known as the Little Hercules. They belong to an early attempt by Landgrave Carl to monumentalise the upper slope of Wilhelmshöhe. Because no complete architecture survives, the site is easy to overlook. Its importance is archaeological and historical rather than visual: it demonstrates that the famous Hercules scheme did not spring fully formed from a single final design. Earlier building campaigns, abandoned ideas and changes of scale preceded the Guerniero project.
kleiner-herkules.history: The official monument inventory records work on an earlier construction, often associated with the Winterkasten, from 1696 and identifies the Little Hercules ruins with this first planning phase. Carl's journey to Italy in 1699/1700 and the arrival of Giovanni Francesco Guerniero in 1701 led to the much more ambitious solution of the present Octagon and cascades. The surviving remains therefore stand at a turning point in the design process.
kleiner-herkules.architecture: What survives is masonry and foundation fabric rather than complete rooms. The low visibility of the remains makes accurate spatial mapping and explanatory graphics especially useful. They should not be confused with later deliberately artificial ruins such as Löwenburg. Little Hercules is an actual remnant of an abandoned or superseded construction phase.
kleiner-herkules.culturalSignificance: The remains are rare material evidence for the design process behind the Baroque park. They challenge the simplified idea of an immutable master plan and show how patronage, travel, architectural advice and construction experimentation changed the final result.
kleiner-herkules.restorationHistory: The ruin fabric is conserved as a protected feature. Intervention is primarily concerned with stabilising and retaining the surviving material rather than recreating an unbuilt or incompletely known superstructure.
kleiner-herkules.visitorContext: The site lies in sloping woodland and is less intensively developed for visitors than the main Hercules monument. Paths may be uneven. Visitors should remain on established routes and should not climb or disturb masonry remains.
kleiner-herkules.interpretation: The strongest interpretation is comparative: the modest 1696-phase remains here can be set against the vast post-1701 Hercules complex nearby. That physical contrast makes planning history tangible. A digital reconstruction may help show proposed or early forms, but any reconstruction must be labelled according to evidence level. The site is valuable precisely because it preserves uncertainty and change in the creative process rather than a complete architectural object.

vexierwassergrotte.name: Vexing Water Grotto
vexierwassergrotte.shortDescription: The Vexing Water Grotto belongs to the Baroque water theatre at the Hercules and used concealed hydraulic effects to surprise and amuse visitors.
vexierwassergrotte.longDescription: The Vexing Water Grotto represents the playful side of Baroque hydraulic display. The German term Vexierwasser refers to water effects intended to surprise, tease or momentarily confuse visitors through jets whose technical cause was hidden. Within the Hercules complex such effects belonged to a larger theatre of grottos, figures, horns, basins and moving water. The fascination came from the contrast between invisible mechanism and apparently spontaneous action. Water became almost a performer in its own right.
vexierwassergrotte.history: The grotto belongs to the early eighteenth-century scheme under Landgrave Carl and Giovanni Francesco Guerniero. UNESCO explicitly mentions the Vexing Grotto as part of the Baroque water programme, making it more than a local curiosity. It belongs to the same integrated work of architecture, hydraulic engineering and courtly representation that underpins the World Heritage inscription.
vexierwassergrotte.architecture: Artificial rockwork and grotto architecture conceal channels, jets and pressure effects. Its operating principle remains consistent with the core historical concept of the Wilhelmshöhe waterworks: gravity rather than modern recirculating pumps.

Jussow’s core structure was built in 1803–1806 for the cascade custodian, while service to park visitors is already documented in the 1820s. The shift from operational residence to hospitality was therefore early and is itself part of the site’s historical biography.

Its position beside the Neptune Basin and at the foot of the Cascades was functional: a technically sensitive part of the waterworks could be supervised from here, while the location also became a natural place of rest and refreshment on the demanding park route. The shed and younger service building belong to the present ensemble but should not be assigned the core building’s date.

aufseherhaus-herkules.name: Custodian’s House at Hercules
aufseherhaus-herkules.shortDescription: The surviving custodian’s house near Hercules is separately inventoried in the UNESCO nomination and must not be merged with the Kaskadenwirtschaft or the ruined Fasanerie custodian’s house.
aufseherhaus-herkules.longDescription: Several buildings in the Bergpark historically carried custodian functions. The UNESCO dossier explicitly separates a Custodian’s House, Hercules Terrace, Hercules visitor centre and Kaskadenwirtschaft among the western ancillary buildings. The local OSM snapshot additionally maps a surviving historic Aufseherhaus at Schlosspark 24 and, farther southeast, the ruins of the Fasanerie custodian’s house. These three meanings are therefore represented by separate nodes.
aufseherhaus-herkules.history: Phase 2 establishes identity, position and inventory status first. A detailed construction history of the surviving house will be added only after a site-specific primary source is available, rather than transferring facts from other custodian houses.
aufseherhaus-herkules.architecture: A surviving historic building; the coordinate is the centroid of the mapped OSM building geometry.
aufseherhaus-herkules.culturalSignificance: The building makes visible the staffing and operational infrastructure required to maintain, supervise and receive visitors around the monumental Hercules area.
aufseherhaus-herkules.restorationHistory: Specific recent restoration dates remain an open research item until confirmed by a primary source.
aufseherhaus-herkules.visitorContext: The house is not a regularly open museum; respect privacy and operational use.
aufseherhaus-herkules.interpretation: The key interpretive point is disambiguation: the Kaskadenwirtschaft, the custodian’s house near Hercules, and the Fasanerie custodian-house ruin are not the same building.

herkules-terrassen.name: Hercules Terraces
herkules-terrassen.shortDescription: The Hercules Terraces are a current gastronomy and service point beside the Hercules monument, separately inventoried in the UNESCO nomination as the western ancillary “Herkulesterrasse”.
herkules-terrassen.longDescription: The node complements the monumental Hercules and Cascade objects with visitor infrastructure that the nomination explicitly inventories. It is not a substitute for the Hercules monument and is not presented as a historic garden staffage. The City of Kassel lists Hercules Terraces among Bergpark gastronomy, while OSM supplies the current named position.
herkules-terrassen.history: No detailed building chronology is asserted without a site-specific primary source. The UNESCO inventory is used to secure spatial distinction from the custodian’s house, visitor centre and Kaskadenwirtschaft.
herkules-terrassen.architecture: A present-day gastronomy site; the coordinate corresponds to the OSM restaurant point.
herkules-terrassen.culturalSignificance: Important for visitor orientation and complete inventory coverage, but of lower cultural-historical rank than Hercules, the Cascades and the historic staffages.
herkules-terrassen.restorationHistory: Operational alterations are not treated as park restoration.
herkules-terrassen.visitorContext: Opening hours are operator-dependent and should be checked before visiting.
herkules-terrassen.interpretation: Separate modelling prevents restaurant, visitor-centre and monument functions at Hercules from collapsing into one POI.
